meta.title: Electrical & Electronics Tooling and Moulding — Metal Form
meta.description: Mould design and manufacture for connector bodies, terminal blocks, switch parts, glands and enclosures. Thin-wall tooling, insert moulds for metal terminals, multi-cavity production and ongoing component supply. Persian engineering since 2006.

name: Electrical & Electronics
tile: Thin-wall housings and connectors, where flow length decides whether the part fills.

headline: The plastic that has
to hold the contact.
hero.lead: Connector bodies, terminal blocks, switch parts, glands, enclosures. Thin walls, deep pockets, metal inserts, and a pitch that still has to be right after a few million shots. Send the part or the drawing. We come back on geometry, tooling route, cavitation and supply.

masthead.caption: Connector body in section. One tick per contact position; copper marks metal, nothing else on this page does.
masthead.combLabel: Pitch comb · one tick per way

parts.heading: Fourteen parts, and the one feature that decides each tool.
parts.body: The part is almost never the product. It is the insulating, locating and retaining half of an assembly whose value sits in the metal and the circuit. Find yours in the list. The line beside it is the geometry that decides whether the tool is right.
parts.colFeature: The feature that decides the tool

rows.name: Connector housings and bodies
rows.feature: Deep slender cores form the terminal pockets. Pitch has to hold across every way and every cavity.

rows.name: Terminal carriers, headers and contact retainers
rows.feature: Retention geometry is the whole function. Flash on a contact face is a reject, not a cosmetic note.

rows.name: Terminal block bodies and covers
rows.feature: Barriers and slots are insulation geometry, not stiffening. Screw bosses take real torque.

rows.name: Switch bodies, rockers, actuators and pivots
rows.feature: Pivot clearance and snap geometry are dimensional. Ejection witness has nowhere cosmetic to hide.

rows.name: Socket and plug shells
rows.feature: Thick and thin in one part. Internal rib layout is fixed by creepage, not by stiffness.

rows.name: Cable glands, gland nuts and cable entries
rows.feature: Threads are moulded, not cut. That is an unscrewing or collapsible-core decision in the tool.

rows.name: Junction boxes, DIN-rail enclosures and lids
rows.feature: Warp decides lid-to-body fit. The rail clip and the sealing lip are the two features that get measured.

rows.name: Device and breaker housings
rows.feature: Left half, right half, cover, actuator — all to one datum. Family tooling is tempting here and often wrong.

rows.name: Coil formers and bobbins
rows.feature: Thin flanges, a tight winding surface, and dimensional stability under the heat of the winding.

rows.name: Light guides and indicator lenses
rows.feature: The mould finish is the optical specification: polished where light stays in, textured where it leaves.

rows.name: Busbar supports, phase barriers and spacers
rows.feature: Simple geometry, unforgiving creepage and clearance, sustained thermal exposure.

rows.name: Cable clips, strain reliefs and retaining clips
rows.feature: Worth a cent. Entirely a cavitation and cycle question, and the first part anyone re-sources.

rows.name: Panels, fascias, buttons and keypad frames
rows.feature: The visible face constrains gate and ejector layout before anything else does.

rows.name: Battery holders, spacers and pack internals
rows.feature: Repeating pockets and thin ribs. The tolerance stacks across the array, not within one pocket.

parts.close: If a rib on your drawing looks like stiffening, ask before you delete it. On an electrical part it is often a creepage barrier, and its length is part of the reason the product passed approval.

wall.heading: Melt travels a fixed distance and then it stops.
wall.body: Flow length divided by wall thickness decides gate count, fill speed, and whether the part fills at all. Published practice puts thin wall below roughly 1 mm, or above a ratio of about 100:1. Thin-wall electrical work commonly runs past 150:1.
wall.body2: Thinner is not automatically cheaper. Cooling time falls and the process window narrows with it. Past a certain ratio the part still fills — but only on a good lot, on a warm tool, on a good day.
wall.colVerdict: What the tool has to do about it

ladder.verdict: Fills on any machine. Gate position is a convenience, not a constraint.
Thin wall begins. Vent depth becomes a dimension on the drawing rather than a fix after the first short shot.
Common on electrical housings. Fill rate and injection pressure carry the part; cavity and core steel must be stiff enough not to deflect under it.
A second gate, or a thicker nominal wall. One of the two has to move, and it is cheaper to decide that before steel.

wall.caption: One cavity, folded. The melt front advances from the gate and the ratio climbs with every millimetre it travels.
wall.note: The 1 mm threshold, the 100:1 and 150:1 bands and the injection pressures behind them are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.
wall.close: We establish the nominal wall and the true flow length before anything else, because every later decision — gate count, runner type, cavitation, steel — is downstream of that one ratio.

weld.heading: Two flows meet somewhere. You decide where.
weld.body: Every core pin, hole and insert splits the melt, and the melt rejoins behind it as a weld line. It cannot be removed. In glass-filled grades the fibres orient along the meeting front instead of bridging it, so the seam approaches the strength of unfilled matrix. That makes weld-line placement structural, not cosmetic.

cases.title: The seam lands in the latch root.
cases.note: Two gates on the short faces. The fronts meet on the centre line and run straight through the one feature that takes an insertion load. The part measures correctly and fractures on service disconnection.

cases.title: The seam lands in plain wall.
cases.note: One gate at the base. The fronts no longer meet under the latch; the only seams left are the two behind the core pins, and they fall where nothing is loaded. What you give up: a single gate raises fill pressure and moves the last-to-fill into the two top corners, so the venting goes there instead.

weld.leversHeading: The five levers, in the order they get forgotten
levers: Sequenced fill on a valve-gated tool, used to walk the meeting point off a feature
Packing pressure at the meeting point
weld.close: The last one is the one nobody remembers. Trapped air compresses and burns at exactly the coordinate where the flows meet, so a weld line and a burn mark are the same event seen twice. A vent cut at design time costs nothing; a vent cut into a running tool costs a week.
weld.caption: Same housing, same core pins, same part print. Only the gate has moved.

insert.heading: The metal is in the tool before the plastic is.
insert.body: Stamped terminals, contacts, pins and threaded bushes, loaded into the cavity and moulded around. The concept is simple. Every problem it creates is dimensional or operational.

stages.label: Load
stages.note: The stamping is placed and located. Its own tolerance arrives with it, and the tool absorbs that variation — not the operator, and not a sorting bench downstream.

stages.label: Close
stages.note: Steel meets metal at the shut-off. Too tight crushes the terminal. Too loose flashes onto the contact face, where flash does not read as cosmetic — it blocks the contact.

stages.label: Shot
stages.note: Melt keys into knurl, groove or undercut. Without one of the three the joint survives moulding and loses grip after thermal cycling, which is a field failure, not a line reject.

stages.label: Eject
stages.note: The part leaves with the metal in it. Sink over the insert and flash in the pocket are the two defects that create a sorting operation nobody ever removes again.

insert.close: At volume the terminals arrive as continuous strip and a dam bar is designed into the frame to stop melt leaking between leads, then punched out afterwards. Loading is where the downtime lives: a mis-seated insert closes the tool onto metal, and that costs more than every part the tool made that month.
insert.boundaryNote: Strip, bandolier and dam-bar practice described here is how the industry runs high-volume terminal overmoulding. Tell us which form your metal arrives in and we will design the shut-off around it.
insert.caption: One tool, four states, the same terminal throughout.

resin.heading: A datasheet property arrives as a steel decision.
resin.body: The compound your approvals file was written around is not the base polymer. Flame-retardant and high-CTI grades flow differently, shrink differently and are usually harder on steel. Shrinkage decides the first cut. Abrasion decides how long that cut stays correct.
columns: What it does to the tool

rows.consequence: Hygroscopic. The part conditions in service and moves. Drying is a process requirement before it is a tooling one.
Anisotropic shrink reads as pitch error across a multi-way body long before it reads as visible distortion. Cut steel-safe wherever a dimension is uncertain.
Takes up more moisture than PA66. Post-mould conditioning is part of the dimension, so the measurement plan has to say when the part was measured.
Freezes sharply. Thin sections need a hot enough tool and a fast enough fill, which makes cooling design and process window one conversation, not two.
Low moisture uptake and stable dimensions, but far higher shrink than the filled grades. Do not carry a filled-grade allowance across.
High melt viscosity, so thin walls need pressure. Notch-sensitive: a sharp internal corner left in the steel becomes a crack in the field.

rows.use: Enclosures and fascias carrying impact and surface
rows.consequence: Flows better than PC. The visible face sets gate and ejector layout before any other consideration does.
Easy to fill and easy to texture. Rarely the grade an approvals file is written around, so check before substituting it.
Very low viscosity: it flashes through gaps that hold every other resin. Shut-off tolerance is effectively the whole build.
Abrasive and hot. Hardened, replaceable gate inserts — not a gate machined straight into the cavity block.
Polish and texture zones are the optical specification and belong on the tool drawing, recorded as functional surfaces.

rows.use: Anything carrying a flame or tracking requirement
rows.consequence: A distinct compound with its own flow and shrink, frequently more aggressive on steel, often with regrind limits. Published halogen-free phosphinate systems in PA and PBT reach CTI values up to 600 V.

resin.note: Shrinkage bands and the 600 V CTI figure are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements. The grade's own datasheet, applied per direction, is what gets cut into steel.
resin.close: Tell us the exact grade, not the polymer family. Two PBT compounds with the same glass loading and different flame-retardant systems will not shrink the same way, and the difference is the difference between an adjustment and a new insert.

pitch.heading: Pitch does not fail. It drifts.
pitch.body: A worn gate does not announce itself. It opens up, fill balance shifts, dimensions move a little, and the parts pass every early inspection. Fourteen months later an assembly line starts rejecting a component that was correct at T1 and has not been changed since.
pitch.detailNote: Retention shoulder and terminal barb, enlarged. The engagement is a few tenths of a millimetre of moulded geometry and it is the whole of terminal retention.

callouts.name: Retention shoulder
callouts.note: The moulded step the contact barb sits under. Terminal retention is verified by the customer under the IEC 60512 test family, and this feature is what it measures.

callouts.name: Contact barb
callouts.note: Stamped, sprung, and working against a surface that has to stay where the tool put it. If the shoulder moulds short or soft, the terminal backs out under vibration.

callouts.name: Core pin
callouts.note: Deep, slender, heat-loaded on every face and deflecting under fill pressure. A pin that wanders makes parts that measure acceptable and assemble badly.

pitch.steelHeading: What holds the dimension is hardness. What goes first is the gate.
pitch.steelBody: Glass fibre sits at Mohs 5 to 7 and abrades steel as the fibres orient along the cavity wall during fill. Gates and high-shear zones erode first, which is why they should be consumables with a change interval rather than cavity surface.

steelRows.use: Unfilled work with a longer expected run.
The default cavity answer for abrasive glass-filled grades, deliberately not taken much above 50 HRC.
Tight-tolerance, long-running parts. Slides and lifters at 54 – 56 HRC against cavities at 50 – 52 HRC.

pitch.steelNote: Steel grades and hardness bands are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements. A ten-point hardness spread run at low hardness invites galling on the sliding faces.
pitch.close: Spare cavity and core inserts and a written condition record are part of the tool, not an afterthought bought later. On a part that stops a line, the interval between a gate wearing and a customer noticing is the whole risk.
pitch.caption: Two adjacent ways at high magnification, with the shoulder detail enlarged beside them.

source.heading: A second source discovered during a shortage is not a second source.
source.body: One tool, one moulder, one country, no duplicate and no spare inserts — on a component worth a few cents that stops a line worth a thousand times more. Building the backup before the shortage is the entire point, and the work is a documentation exercise before it is a machining one.

stages.title: NDA, then the part
stages.note: A sample, a STEP file, a 2D drawing, or a photograph with one dimension we can scale from. An NDA can be signed before detailed disclosure if you prefer.

stages.title: Data pack
stages.note: Current CAD, 2D with tolerances, material grade, known process parameters, acceptance criteria. What exists — and, more usefully, what does not.

stages.title: DFM review
stages.note: Wall, flow length, gate and weld-line placement, draft, ejection, shrink allowance per grade. Before any steel is quoted.

stages.title: Tooling route
stages.note: A duplicate built from your data, or a new tool built to your part print. Where the drawings and the original toolmaker are both gone, reverse engineering from a sample.

stages.title: Build
stages.note: Mould design and manufacture in CATIA and SolidWorks. Multi-cavity, hot or cold runner, insert tooling, slides, lifters, unscrewing and collapsible cores as the part requires.

stages.title: T1 and qualification
stages.note: First shots measured against parts you already accept, not against an idealised print. Corrections are cheap here and expensive everywhere after here.

stages.title: Scheduled supply
stages.note: Component production and rolling supply, in the same box to the same spec, with international delivery and spares and change parts held against the tool.

source.close: This is readiness, not reserved capacity. Capacity is reserved by contract or it is not reserved at all, and we will tell you which one you are being offered.
source.warranty: Tooling warranty terms are defined per project and against the agreed mould specification. Initial technical response within 2 business days.

boundary.heading: We do not certify anything electrical.
boundary.body: In this sector the buyer's real anxiety is approval, and the honest answer is a boundary rather than a claim. Flame and tracking ratings belong to the resin grade and to your finished-product approval. They do not belong to the moulder, and a supplier who implies otherwise has not been through an approvals process.
doList: Mould design and manufacture: injection, PET, blow and die-cast tooling, multi-cavity, hot and cold runner, insert tooling.
Slides, lifters, unscrewing and collapsible cores for latch windows, side apertures and moulded gland threads.
DFM review of an existing part or drawing before any steel is quoted.
Reverse engineering from a sample or a photograph where the drawings are gone.
Second-source and duplicate tooling, plus spares and change parts.
CNC milling, turning and manual machining.
Component production, rolling supply and international delivery.
Moulding in the grade you specify, to the geometry you specify.
NDA before detailed disclosure, and tooling warranty on terms defined per project.
A written note whenever a geometry change we propose would shorten a creepage path, so it reaches your approvals process instead of your production line.
dontList: UL listing, a UL file or a UL Yellow Card. We hold none and we will not appear on yours as a test source.
UL94 flammability, CTI tracking, glow-wire and dielectric testing. We do not perform any of it.
IEC 60664, IEC 60512, IEC 60335 or any other electrical safety testing, declaration or certification.
Selection and approval of the resin grade. Flame and tracking ratings are properties of the compound you specify.
Approval of the finished product, and the decision on any geometry change that touches a creepage or clearance path.
Verification of terminal retention, dielectric withstand and every other electrical figure on your specification.
boundary.close: That list is not fine print. It is the shape of the working relationship: you own the electrical performance and the approval, we own the geometry, the steel and the supply. Where the two meet — a rib that is a creepage barrier, a weld line under an insertion load, a gate vestige on a mating face — we raise it before we quote, not after.

items.title: Thin wall, in numbers
bullets: Thin wall begins below roughly 1 mm, or above a flow-length-to-thickness ratio of about 100:1.
Thin-wall electrical parts commonly run past 150:1. The ratio, not the thickness alone, is the constraint.
High fill rate and high injection pressure are required, with figures up to around 35,000 psi quoted for thin-wall work.
Venting is a designed feature at that speed, not a correction applied after the first short shot.
Cavity and core steel must be stiff enough not to deflect under fill, which limits how slender a core can be made.
Cooling has to be fitted into the thin steel between pockets. Baffles, bubblers and high-conductivity core inserts do more for cycle and consistency than adding circuits to the plate.
Uneven core temperature produces uneven shrink, and uneven shrink in a multi-way body reads as pitch error.
items.source: Figures in this panel are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

items.title: Insert moulding checkpoints
bullets: Confirm the incoming stamping's tolerance and locating features with the stamper before the shut-off is designed.
The shut-off must absorb insert variation without flashing onto contact faces and without crushing the metal.
Give the polymer something to key into — knurl, groove or undercut — so the joint survives thermal cycling.
At volume, terminals arrive as continuous strip; dam bars are designed into the frame to stop leakage between leads and punched out afterwards.
Loading is where the downtime lives: a mis-seated insert closes the tool onto metal.
Sink over an insert and flash in a terminal pocket are the two defects that create permanent sorting operations.
Incoming stamping variation is also what stops an automated loading cell, so the tolerance conversation is a throughput conversation.
items.source: Described as industry practice. Tell us the form your metal arrives in and the shut-off is designed around it.

items.title: Tolerance and the mating feature
bullets: Pitch across a multi-way body is the dimension that decides whether the part mates.
Glass-filled grades shrink less along fibre orientation than across it, so warp presents as pitch error before it presents as visible distortion.
Cavity-to-cavity variation in a high-cavitation tool matters more than absolute accuracy in any single cavity — parts within one shot have to be interchangeable.
Terminal retention is set by moulded retaining geometry and verified by the customer under the IEC 60512 test family.
Gate vestige standing proud on a mating, sealing or optical face is a functional defect, and that is what drives gate-type selection.
We publish no tolerance figures here. The achievable band is a function of the geometry, the grade and the tool, and it is stated per project.
On sub-gram parts a cold runner can weigh more than the parts it feeds, so runner strategy is an annual resin bill rather than a tooling preference.
items.source: Figures and test-standard references in this panel are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

cta.headline: Send the part. We will tell you what the tool has to do.
cta.body: A STEP file, a 2D drawing, or a sample in a bag. We come back on geometry, tooling route, cavitation and supply options. Initial project response within 2 business days. NDA on request, before you send anything.
